slides.text: You know what capacity is. Now you will use it: make a slice with the room it needs, tell when an append moved the values, reuse a buffer, and let go of a big slice you only needed a piece of.

When you know how many values you will add, make the slice with length 0 and the capacity you need. Every `append` then fits, and the slice never has to move to a bigger place.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
list shows 0, room for 4
append 1 -> shows 1, room for 4
append 2 -> shows 2, room for 4

slides.text: Do not mix up the two forms. `make([]int, 3)` already shows 3 zeros, and `append` adds after them. `make([]int, 0, 3)` shows nothing and has room for 3.

exercises.title: Make room, then append
exercises.guide: Build a slice in a loop with its room made first.

chunks.guide: Every append fits, so the capacity never changes.

exercises.title: Length or capacity
exercises.guide: Compare the two ways of calling make.

chunks.guide: The 3 is a length here: the slice already holds 3 zeros.
chunks.text:
filled := make([]int, 3)
    filled = append(filled, 7)
    fmt.Println(filled, len(filled))

chunks.guide: Here the 3 is only room, so the slice starts empty.
chunks.text:
roomy := make([]int, 0, 3)
    roomy = append(roomy, 7)
    fmt.Println(roomy, len(roomy), cap(roomy))

exercises.title: Make room for the labels
exercises.guide: Make `labels` empty with room for every name, then add each label to it.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `make([]int, size)` starts with 3 zeros, and the loop adds 0, 1 and 2 after them.

exercises.title: Make room in a function
exercises.guide: Return a slice built with the room it needs.

chunks.guide: The function knows it will keep at most half the numbers, so it makes that room.

notes.text: Half the limit is room enough for the evens.

chunks.guide: Here the room is used up exactly.

exercises.title: Grow by cutting
exercises.guide: Make the slice longer without append.

chunks.guide: Empty, with room for 4. A cut can show 2 of those places.
chunks.text:
buf := make([]int, 0, 4)
    buf = buf[:2]
    buf[0] = 1
    buf[1] = 2
    fmt.Println(buf, len(buf), cap(buf))

chunks.guide: Cutting up to the capacity shows the rest of the room, still zero.

notes.text: Stretches the length to use all the room.

slides.text:
After an `append`, the code does not say whether the slice got new values or reused the old ones. You can find out without printing the capacity: change a value through one slice and see whether the other one notices.

When there is no room, Go makes a bigger stretch, usually about double for small slices. The exact size is up to Go, so a program should not count on it.

A cut keeps the whole stretch of values alive, even when it shows only two of them. A small piece of a huge slice holds all that memory. To let go of the big one, copy the piece into a slice of its own.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
big = 1000 values
small = first 2 of big (holds 1000)
keep = new list, a copy of those 2

exercises.title: Who still shares
exercises.guide: Find out which appends made new values.

chunks.guide: Room for 3, and an append that fits.
chunks.text:
items := make([]int, 2, 3)
    withOne := append(items, 1)
    withOne[0] = 9
    fmt.Println(items[0], withOne[0])

chunks.guide: Now `withOne` is full, so this append makes new values. A change to `withTwo` stays in `withTwo`.
The new stretch is bigger than the old one.

exercises.title: Spare room in a function
exercises.guide: Append inside a function that has room to spare.

chunks.guide: The function appends to its own copy of the slice.
The caller still shows 2 values. But the 9 was written into the room behind them.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    full := make([]int, 2, 2)
    grown := append(full, 1)
    full[0] = 7
    fmt.Println(grown[0], cap(full))
}
exercises.explanation: `full` is full, so `grown` has its own values and the change to `full` does not reach it. `full` keeps its capacity of 2.

exercises.title: Let go of the big slice
exercises.guide: Keep a few values without holding the rest.

chunks.guide: A small piece still has the room of the whole slice.
chunks.text:
big := make([]int, 1000)
    small := big[:2]
    fmt.Println(len(small), cap(small))

chunks.guide: A copy has its own values, and only as much room as it needs.
chunks.text:
keep := make([]int, 2)
    copy(keep, big[:2])
    fmt.Println(len(keep), cap(keep))

exercises.title: Keep only the head
exercises.guide: Make `keep` as long as `part`, and copy the values of `part` into it.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    big := make([]int, 50)
    part := big[:3]
    keep := make([]int, ___(part))
    ___(keep, part)
    fmt.Println(cap(part), cap(keep))
}

exercises.title: Reuse the room
exercises.guide: Empty a slice and fill it again in the same place.

chunks.guide: Fill the room, and keep a second name for the same values.
chunks.text:
buf := make([]int, 0, 3)
    buf = append(buf, 1, 2, 3)
    old := buf

chunks.guide: Cutting to length 0 keeps the room, so the next append writes over the first value.
chunks.text:
buf = buf[:0]
    buf = append(buf, 9)
    fmt.Println(buf, old)
